title: How Much Alcohol Is in Beer, Wine, and Liquor? ABV Chart by Drink
excerpt: How much alcohol is in beer, wine, liquor, hard seltzer, and cocktails? A plain-English ABV chart, standard-drink math, and the pours that catch people out.
metaDescription: How much alcohol is in beer, wine, and liquor? ABV chart by drink, standard-drink math, and the strong beers and big pours that add up fast.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how much alcohol is in beer
content:
**The quick answer:** a regular 12-ounce beer has about 5% alcohol by volume, which works out to roughly 0.6 fluid ounces (about 14 grams) of pure alcohol. That's one US "standard drink." Light beers sit a little lower, around 4% to 4.2%, and craft IPAs often run 6% to 7.5%, with double IPAs and imperial stouts going to 8% to 12% or more. A 5-ounce glass of 12% wine and a 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor contain about the same amount of alcohol as that regular beer. The size of the pour and the strength printed on the label matter far more than whether the drink is beer, wine, or liquor.

This guide gives you a reference chart for the most common drinks, explains how to work out the real alcohol in any glass in about ten seconds, and covers the places people most often get caught out: tall cans, strong craft beer, generous wine pours, and mixed drinks.

> **A note on safety:** the numbers here are averages for planning and comparison, not a way to judge whether you're fit to drive. The same amount of alcohol affects people very differently depending on body size, sex, food, medications, and how fast you drink. If you're going to drive, the only safe number is zero. If someone has had a lot to drink and is confused, vomiting while drowsy, breathing slowly or irregularly, has cold or bluish skin, or can't be woken, call 911 (or your local emergency number). That's possible alcohol poisoning, and it needs care right away, not time to sleep it off.

## What ABV Means and Why It's the Number That Matters

**ABV** stands for **alcohol by volume**. It's the share of the liquid that is pure alcohol (ethanol). A beer labeled 5% ABV is 5% alcohol and 95% everything else: water, carbohydrates, flavor compounds, and carbonation.

ABV on its own doesn't tell you how much alcohol you're drinking. You need two numbers:

1. **How strong the drink is** (the ABV on the label or menu)
2. **How much of it you pour** (the volume in the glass, can, or bottle)

Multiply them together and you get the amount of pure alcohol. A small glass of strong wine can hold more alcohol than a large glass of light beer. That's why "I only had beer" or "it was just wine" doesn't say much about how much you actually drank.

You'll also see **proof** on spirits labels in the US. Proof is simply ABV times two, so 80-proof vodka is 40% ABV, and 100-proof bourbon is 50% ABV.

## What Counts as One Standard Drink

In the United States, a **standard drink** is any drink containing about **14 grams (0.6 fluid ounces) of pure alcohol**. This is the definition used by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), and it's what doctors and US health guidance mean when they talk about "a drink." The classic examples are:

- **12 ounces of regular beer** at about 5% ABV
- **5 ounces of table wine** at about 12% ABV
- **1.5 ounces of distilled spirits** at 40% ABV (80 proof)
- **8 to 9 ounces of malt liquor** at about 7% ABV

Each of those contains roughly the same amount of alcohol. The catch is that real drinks rarely match those textbook sizes. A pint glass is 16 ounces, a restaurant wine pour is often 6 ounces or more, and a home-poured cocktail can easily contain two or three shots.

Other countries use different sizes, which is worth knowing if you read health advice from abroad. The UK counts in **units** of 8 grams (10 ml) of pure alcohol, so a US standard drink is a bit under two UK units. Australia uses a 10-gram standard drink, as do many other countries. Canada uses a standard drink of about 13.5 grams, close to the US figure. When you compare guidelines from different places, check which "drink" they mean.

## Alcohol Content Chart: Common Drinks at a Glance

The table below shows typical ABV ranges and how many US standard drinks a common serving contains. Brands and batches vary, so use this as a starting point and check the label when you can.

| Drink | Typical ABV | Common serving | Approx. standard drinks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-alcoholic beer | 0% to 0.5% | 12 oz | Close to 0 |
| Light beer | 4% to 4.2% | 12 oz | About 0.8 |
| Regular lager | 4.5% to 5% | 12 oz | About 1 |
| Regular lager, pint | 5% | 16 oz | About 1.3 |
| IPA / pale ale | 5.5% to 7.5% | 12 oz | 1.1 to 1.5 |
| IPA, pint | 7% | 16 oz | About 1.9 |
| Double IPA, imperial stout, Belgian strong ale | 8% to 12% | 12 oz | 1.6 to 2.4 |
| Hard seltzer | 4.5% to 5% (some 8%) | 12 oz | About 1 (up to 1.6) |
| Hard cider | 4.5% to 7% | 12 oz | 0.9 to 1.4 |
| Malt liquor | 6% to 8% | 24 oz | 2.4 to 3.2 |
| Table wine | 11% to 14% | 5 oz | 0.9 to 1.2 |
| Restaurant wine pour | 13% | 6 to 9 oz | 1.3 to 2 |
| Bottle of wine | 12% to 14% | 750 ml (25.4 oz) | 5 to 6 |
| Sparkling wine / Champagne | 11% to 12.5% | 5 oz | About 1 |
| Fortified wine (port, sherry) | 15% to 20% | 3 oz | 0.8 to 1 |
| Sake | 14% to 16% | 6 oz | About 1.5 |
| Soju | 12% to 20% | 360 ml bottle | About 2.5 to 4 |
| Liqueurs (cream, coffee) | 15% to 30% | 1.5 oz | 0.4 to 0.8 |
| Vodka, gin, rum, tequila, whiskey | 40% (80 proof) | 1.5 oz shot | 1 |
| Bourbon, bottled-in-bond | 50% (100 proof) | 1.5 oz | About 1.25 |
| Cask-strength whiskey | 55% to 65% | 1.5 oz | 1.4 to 1.6 |

Two rows in that table surprise most people. A single strong craft beer can equal two regular beers, and a bottle of wine split between two people is about two and a half drinks each, not "a glass or two."

## How Much Alcohol Is in Beer?

Most mainstream American lagers sit right around **4.5% to 5% ABV**, which is why a 12-ounce can is the reference point for one standard drink. But "beer" covers a huge range, from under 4% to over 12%, and the style tells you a lot.

### Light beer vs. regular beer

The big US light beers are generally brewed to about **4.2% ABV**, and the flagship regular lagers to about **5%**. That gap is smaller than many people expect. Light beer has fewer calories, mostly because it has fewer leftover carbohydrates, but it is not "barely alcoholic." Four light beers contain a bit more alcohol than three regular beers.

Some imported lagers sit in between, around 4.4% to 4.6%. Irish dry stouts like Guinness Draught are often assumed to be strong because they're dark and heavy-looking, but they're typically brewed at about 4.2%, the same as a light lager. Color tells you about the malt, not the alcohol.

### Craft beer, IPAs, and strong styles

Craft beer is where alcohol content climbs. Rough ranges by style:

- **Session beers and kölsch:** about 3.5% to 5%
- **Pale ales:** about 5% to 6%
- **IPAs:** about 6% to 7.5%
- **Double or imperial IPAs:** about 8% to 10%
- **Belgian dubbels and tripels:** about 7% to 10%
- **Imperial stouts and barleywines:** about 9% to 12%, sometimes higher

A 16-ounce can of 8% double IPA has a little over **two standard drinks** in it. That's the single most common way people drink more than they meant to at a brewery: the glasses look the same as the light lager at home, but each one counts double.

Strong beers also tend to have more residual sugar and more of the flavorful by-products of fermentation, which is one reason they can feel heavier the next morning. If beer in particular tends to leave you rough, our guide to the [beer hangover](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) explains what's going on.

### Does beer on draft or in cans have different alcohol?

No. The same beer has the same ABV whether it's in a can, bottle, or on tap. What changes is the **pour size**. Bars may serve 12-ounce, 14-ounce, 16-ounce, or 20-ounce glasses, and imperial pints in British-style pubs are 20 ounces. A 20-ounce pour of a 5% lager is about 1.7 standard drinks.

### How much alcohol is in a tall can or 40?

A "tallboy" is usually 16 ounces, and some single-serve cans are 19.2, 24, or 25 ounces. A 24-ounce can of 5% beer holds two standard drinks. Malt liquor in a 40-ounce bottle at 7% to 8% holds roughly **four and a half to five and a half standard drinks**, close to half a bottle of wine. Some flavored malt beverages sold in tall single cans run well above 10% ABV, which can put a single can at four or five standard drinks. Always read the label on these.

## How Much Alcohol Is in Wine?

Most still table wines fall between **11% and 14.5% ABV**. A standard 5-ounce glass at 12% is one standard drink, but two things push the real number up: wines are getting stronger, and pours are getting bigger.

### Wine strength by style

- **Lower-alcohol wines (about 5% to 10%):** Moscato d'Asti, many German Rieslings, Portuguese vinho verde, some off-dry rosés
- **Middle range (about 11.5% to 13.5%):** many Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc, Chianti, Beaujolais, and cooler-climate reds
- **Higher range (about 13.5% to 15.5%):** warm-climate Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, Syrah/Shiraz, Grenache, and Zinfandel
- **Sparkling wine and Champagne:** usually about 11% to 12.5%
- **Fortified wines (port, sherry, Madeira, Marsala):** about 15% to 20%, because spirit is added during production
- **Vermouth:** about 15% to 18%

Riper grapes contain more sugar, and yeast turns that sugar into alcohol. That's why wines from hot regions and hot years usually come out stronger.

### Wine labels aren't exact

In the US, wine labels are allowed some leeway on the stated alcohol. For wines at 14% or under, the actual alcohol can differ from the label by up to 1.5 percentage points, and by up to 1 point for wines over 14%. A bottle labeled 13.5% might really be 14.5%. That's not a big deal for one glass, but it adds up over a bottle.

### Your glass is probably bigger than 5 ounces

A 5-ounce pour looks small in a modern wine glass. Many restaurants pour 6 ounces as standard, and pours at home are often 7 to 9 ounces without anyone noticing. A 9-ounce glass of 14% Zinfandel is a little over two standard drinks. A standard 750 ml bottle at 13% holds about **five and a half standard drinks**.

If wine gives you headaches in particular, that's a separate story from alcohol content. See our guides on the [wine hangover](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) and [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache).

## How Much Alcohol Is in Liquor?

Most spirits sold in the US are bottled at **40% ABV (80 proof)**. That includes most vodka, gin, white and spiced rum, tequila, and many whiskeys. A 1.5-ounce shot at 40% is one standard drink.

Common exceptions:

- **Bourbon and rye at higher proof:** bottled-in-bond whiskey is 50% (100 proof); many bourbons sit between 43% and 50%
- **Cask-strength or barrel-proof whiskey:** often 55% to 65%
- **Navy-strength gin:** about 57%
- **Overproof rum:** "151" rums are 75.5% ABV
- **Grain alcohol:** some neutral grain spirits are sold at 95% (190 proof), which is more than twice the strength of regular vodka
- **Flavored whiskeys and spirit-based "shots":** often lower, around 30% to 35%
- **Liqueurs:** cream liqueurs are about 15% to 17%, coffee liqueurs about 20%, while orange liqueurs like triple sec range from about 15% up to 40%

A shot glass isn't a fixed size either. In the US, shot glasses run from about 1 ounce to 2 ounces, and a "double" is usually 2 to 3 ounces. A free pour at a party is often closer to 2 ounces than 1.5.

Clear and dark spirits at the same proof contain the same amount of alcohol. Darker spirits like bourbon and brandy do carry more **congeners** (other compounds formed during fermentation and aging), which may make hangovers worse for some people. Our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) covers that research.

## How Much Alcohol Is in Hard Seltzer, Cider, and Other Drinks?

### Hard seltzer

Most mainstream hard seltzers are **4.5% to 5% ABV** in a 12-ounce can, so they're about one standard drink each, the same as a regular beer. Some "higher-ABV" lines run 8%, which makes each can about 1.6 drinks. Hard seltzers taste light and go down easily, which makes them easy to drink faster than beer. The alcohol is the same; the pace often isn't. More on that in our [hard seltzer hangover guide](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

### Hard cider

Most ciders are **4.5% to 7%**, with some "imperial" or ice ciders much stronger. A 16-ounce can of 6.9% cider is about 1.8 standard drinks.

### Hard kombucha

Hard kombucha usually runs about **4.5% to 7%**. Regular store-bought kombucha is sold as non-alcoholic and is kept under 0.5%.

### Sake and soju

**Sake** is typically **14% to 16%**, a bit stronger than most wine. A 6-ounce carafe pour is about one and a half drinks. **Soju** varies a lot: many popular green-bottle brands are about 12% to 17%, while traditional versions can be 20% or stronger. A whole 360 ml bottle of soju at 16% contains a little over three standard drinks, and those bottles are often shared casually over a long meal. See our [sake hangover guide](/never-hungover/sake-hangover) if that's your drink.

### Non-alcoholic beer and wine

In the US, drinks labeled "non-alcoholic" can contain up to **0.5% ABV**, and "alcohol-free" or "0.0" products should have essentially none. At 0.5%, you'd need to drink about ten 12-ounce cans to take in the alcohol of one regular beer, and your body clears it about as fast as it arrives. That said, people who need to avoid alcohol completely (during pregnancy, with certain medications, or in recovery) should choose 0.0 products and talk to their doctor if unsure.

## How Much Alcohol Is in a Cocktail?

Cocktails are the hardest drinks to estimate because there's no label and the recipe depends on who's pouring. The rule of thumb: count the ounces of spirit and liqueur, and ignore the mixers.

Approximate alcohol content of common cocktails, using typical bar recipes with 80-proof spirits:

| Cocktail | Typical alcohol in it | Approx. standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| Vodka soda, gin and tonic, rum and Coke | 1.5 oz spirit | 1 |
| Same, made as a "double" | 3 oz spirit | 2 |
| Margarita | 2 oz tequila + 0.5 to 1 oz orange liqueur | 1.5 to 2 |
| Martini | 2 to 2.5 oz gin or vodka + vermouth | 1.5 to 2 |
| Old Fashioned / Manhattan | 2 oz whiskey (+ vermouth for a Manhattan) | 1.3 to 2 |
| Mojito | 1.5 to 2 oz rum | 1 to 1.3 |
| Long Island iced tea | About 2.5 to 3 oz combined spirits and liqueur | About 1.7 to 2 |
| Frozen or "fishbowl" drinks | Highly variable | Often 2 to 4 or more |

Drinks like the Long Island iced tea taste mild because of the sugar and cola but contain four or five different spirits. Punch bowls and party batches are even harder to judge, since you have no idea how much liquor went in. If you're drinking from a batch, assume each cup is stronger than it tastes.

Cocktails made with carbonated mixers, like vodka soda, may also raise blood alcohol a little faster than the same alcohol in a non-fizzy drink, because carbonation can speed the passage of alcohol from the stomach into the small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. The effect isn't large or consistent in every study, but it's another reason fizzy drinks can "hit" faster.

## How to Work Out the Alcohol in Any Drink

You can calculate the number of US standard drinks in anything with a single line of math:

**Standard drinks = ounces × ABV ÷ 0.6**

Use the ABV as a decimal (5% = 0.05). Some examples:

- **16 oz IPA at 7%:** 16 × 0.07 = 1.12 oz of alcohol. 1.12 ÷ 0.6 = **about 1.9 drinks**
- **8 oz glass of wine at 14%:** 8 × 0.14 = 1.12 oz. 1.12 ÷ 0.6 = **about 1.9 drinks**
- **2 oz pour of 100-proof bourbon:** 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 oz. 1.0 ÷ 0.6 = **about 1.7 drinks**
- **12 oz light beer at 4.2%:** 12 × 0.042 = 0.5 oz. 0.5 ÷ 0.6 = **about 0.84 drinks**

If you think in milliliters, the equivalent is: **ml × ABV × 0.789 = grams of alcohol**, then divide by 14 for US standard drinks (or by 8 for UK units). The 0.789 is the density of ethanol, which converts volume to weight.

A quick sanity check: a 750 ml bottle of 40% vodka contains about 237 grams of alcohol, or roughly **17 standard drinks**.

## Why the Same Number of Drinks Hits People Differently

Knowing the alcohol content of a drink tells you the dose. It doesn't tell you how that dose will feel, because your blood alcohol level depends on a lot more than the drink:

- **Body size and composition.** Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A smaller person, or someone with a higher share of body fat, has less water to dilute it into, so the same drink produces a higher concentration.
- **Sex.** On average, women reach a higher blood alcohol level than men after the same amount of alcohol, partly because of body water and partly because of differences in how alcohol is broken down in the stomach.
- **Food.** Alcohol is absorbed much faster on an empty stomach. Eating a real meal beforehand slows absorption and lowers the peak. Our guide to [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) goes through which foods help most.
- **Pace.** Your liver processes alcohol at a fairly steady rate, on average about one standard drink per hour, though this varies widely between people. Three drinks in one hour lands very differently than three drinks over three hours.
- **Medications.** Many common medications, including sleep aids, antihistamines, some antidepressants, and pain medicines, add to alcohol's effects or interact with it. Check with a pharmacist if you're unsure about anything you take.
- **Genetics.** Some people, especially many of East Asian descent, carry variants that slow the breakdown of acetaldehyde, a toxic intermediate of alcohol metabolism. That's what causes facial flushing, a racing heart, and nausea after small amounts.

This is also why nothing on this page can tell you whether you're safe to drive. Estimate tools and calculators give a ballpark at best.

## How Much Is "Moderate" Drinking in These Terms?

US dietary guidance has long described moderate drinking as up to **one drink a day for women and up to two for men**, on days when people drink. Those numbers refer to standard drinks, not glasses. A single large pour of strong wine or one double IPA can use up a full day's "moderate" amount on its own.

Many health organizations now stress that less is better for long-term health, and that there's no level of drinking that's completely risk-free. The NIAAA describes **binge drinking** as a pattern that brings blood alcohol to 0.08% or above, which for a typical adult usually means about **five or more drinks for men or four or more for women within about two hours**. Using the chart above, that's a lot easier to reach than it sounds: three pints of IPA or two large glasses of wine and a cocktail can get you there.

This guide isn't about telling you how much to drink. It's about making sure the number in your head matches the number in your glass.

## Practical Ways to Keep Track

A few simple habits make a big difference:

1. **Check the can, bottle, or menu for ABV.** Many bars list it on the beer menu. If they don't, ask.
2. **Count strong beers and big pours as more than one.** A 16-ounce 7% IPA is about two drinks. A big glass of red is often closer to two than one.
3. **Pour your own wine and spirits with a measure** once or twice. Most people are surprised by how much a "normal" pour really is.
4. **Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.** It slows your pace and helps with hydration.
5. **Eat a proper meal first.** Protein, fat, and fiber slow how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
6. **Be extra careful with batch drinks and sweet cocktails.** They're the easiest to underestimate.
7. **Plan your ride before you start.** Decide how you're getting home while your judgment is at its best.

Lower-strength options are an easy swap if you want to keep the social side without the full dose: session beers, light beers, spritzers made with half wine and half soda water, lower-alcohol wines, or good non-alcoholic beer.

## Alcohol Content and Hangovers

The amount of alcohol is the biggest single driver of how bad a hangover is. More alcohol means more acetaldehyde for your body to clear, more disrupted sleep, more fluid loss, and more irritation to your stomach. Two people who both had "four drinks" can have very different mornings if one had four light beers and the other had four pints of double IPA.

Other factors matter too: congeners, sugar, how much you slept, and how much water you drank. But if you want the most reliable way to feel better the next day, it's keeping track of the real alcohol you drink and pacing it. The old "beer before liquor" rhyme doesn't hold up well; what matters is the total. Our piece on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) explains why, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the rest of the evidence.

## Where DHM Fits (Honestly)

Some people who drink socially also take **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Research, mostly in animals with only limited human data so far, suggests it may support the body's processing of alcohol and acetaldehyde and may help protect the liver. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol level, makes strong drinks "count" for less, or makes it safe to drive. It doesn't change anything in the chart above.

If you want to try it, a plain, well-tested option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts. Think of it as a possible extra, not a substitute for counting your drinks, eating, and drinking water.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How much alcohol is in a 12-ounce beer?**

A regular 12-ounce beer at about 5% ABV contains about 0.6 fluid ounces (14 grams) of pure alcohol, which is one US standard drink. A light beer at about 4.2% has a little less, roughly 0.84 of a drink, while a 7% IPA in the same size has about 1.4 drinks.

**Is one beer the same as one shot?**

Roughly, yes, if the beer is a regular 12-ounce beer at about 5% and the shot is 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. Both contain about 14 grams of alcohol. A strong craft beer, a pint glass, or a heavy-handed pour changes the comparison quickly.

**How many standard drinks are in a bottle of wine?**

A 750 ml bottle at 12% ABV holds about five standard drinks. At 13.5% to 14%, it's closer to five and a half or six. Split between two people, that's at least two and a half drinks each.

**Does light beer have less alcohol?**

Yes, but not by much. Most major US light beers are about 4.2% ABV compared with about 5% for their regular versions, so a light beer has roughly 15% to 20% less alcohol. The bigger difference is in calories and carbohydrates.

**Which beer has the most alcohol?**

Among widely available styles, imperial stouts, barleywines, Belgian strong ales, and double or triple IPAs are the strongest, typically 8% to 12%, and some specialty beers go well beyond that. Mainstream lagers usually sit around 4% to 5%.

**Does dark beer have more alcohol than light-colored beer?**

Not necessarily. Color comes from roasted malt, not alcohol. Guinness Draught, for example, is around 4.2% ABV, about the same as a light lager, while a pale-colored Belgian tripel can be 9% or more.

**How do I calculate how many drinks I've had?**

Multiply the ounces by the ABV (as a decimal), then divide by 0.6. For example, a 16-ounce beer at 6% is 16 × 0.06 ÷ 0.6 = 1.6 standard drinks. Add them up across the night for a realistic total.

**Can I use alcohol content to figure out if I'm OK to drive?**

No. How alcohol affects you depends on your weight, sex, food, pace, medications, and more, so the same number of drinks gives different blood alcohol levels in different people. Impairment starts well before the legal limit. If you've been drinking, don't drive; use a ride service, a sober driver, or public transit.
